nameStory: The name "haddock" comes from the Middle English "haddok," which likely derives from an Old French word. This fish has been so important to coastal communities for centuries that its name has remained remarkably unchanged across languages and time.
description: The haddock is a medium-sized saltwater fish that's a close cousin to the famous cod. These silvery-gray fish typically grow 1-3 feet long and have a distinctive arched back that gives them a somewhat humpbacked appearance. They're most famous for ending up on dinner plates, especially as the delicious smoked "finnan haddie" that New England coastal communities have enjoyed for generations.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark lateral line running along a silvery-gray body with a distinctive large dark blotch (called the "devil's thumbprint") just above the pectoral fin

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Noticeably arched back creating a humpbacked profile, with a streamlined but deep body that feels firm and muscular to the touch

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small terminal mouth positioned at the front of a pointed snout, with a small chin barbel (whisker-like projection) that feels like a short, stiff thread

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Three separate dorsal fins and two anal fins, with the first dorsal fin being triangular and prominently tall

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically 14-23 inches long when caught, with a solid, hefty feel that's noticeably denser than most fish of similar length

habitat: Haddock live in the cold saltwater of the North Atlantic, typically found over sandy or muddy ocean bottoms at depths of 130-450 feet. In New England waters, they prefer the continental shelf areas offshore, especially around Georges Bank and the Gulf of Maine. Unlike their cod cousins, haddock tend to school together in large groups and prefer slightly deeper, more offshore waters.

seasonality.spring: Spawning season brings haddock into slightly shallower waters, making them more accessible to recreational anglers. This is when you're most likely to encounter them closer to shore.
seasonality.summer: Adults move to deeper, cooler waters offshore. Commercial fishing activity peaks as haddock form large schools over preferred feeding grounds.
seasonality.fall: Haddock begin moving back toward their wintering areas. The flesh is considered at its peak quality as fish have been feeding heavily through summer.
seasonality.winter: Found in their deepest waters of the year, typically beyond the reach of most recreational anglers. Commercial trawlers continue to target overwintering schools.

funFact: The distinctive dark spot above a haddock's pectoral fin is called the "devil's thumbprint" in maritime folklore - legend says the devil grabbed the first haddock with his thumb and forefinger, leaving permanent marks that have been passed down through every generation since!
confusionNotes: Haddock are most often confused with cod, but remember: haddock have that distinctive dark "thumbprint" spot and a much more arched back, while cod are more torpedo-shaped and lack the prominent spot. Think "haddock has a hump and a thumbprint."
contextualKnowledge: When you see "finnan haddie" or "smoked haddock" on a New England restaurant menu, you're looking at this exact species prepared in a traditional Scottish smoking method that Maritime communities brought to North America. The yellow color of some smoked haddock comes from artificial dye - naturally smoked haddock is pale gold to white.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus Melanogrammus, haddock are unique among their cod family relatives. Compared to Atlantic cod, haddock have a more pronounced arch to their back, a smaller mouth, and that diagnostic dark shoulder spot that cod lack. Unlike pollock (another cod family member), haddock have a pale lateral line rather than a straight dark one.
